title: US Sanctions Iran's Remaining Shadow Fleet as Hormuz Traffic Hits Wartime Low
subhead: Treasury designated 17 tankers in its 'Operation Economic Outcast' campaign, claiming it has neutralized most of Iran's remaining shadow fleet, while only a single commodity vessel left Hormuz on Wednesday and Europe's gas price jumped 4% on blocked LNG.

sections.heading: Treasury Moves Against the Shadow Fleet's Last Nodes
sections.body:
On October 8, the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control designated 17 vessels in Iran's 'shadow fleet' along with 13 shipping companies, part of the campaign known as 'Operation Economic Outcast,' announced by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on August 24 and dubbed 'Economic D-Day.' A Treasury press release states the action 'effectively neutralizes the vast majority of Iran's remaining shadow fleet network.'

The designations are wide-ranging: the Panama-flagged STARWAY, owned by China-based Hechuang International Group, has moved over three million barrels of Iranian naphtha since 2025; the Marshall Islands-owned crude tanker SHENZHEN over 3.5 million barrels of Iranian crude since November 2025; the Hong Kong-linked AVA 6 over one million barrels of naphtha. The vessels are flagged across more than a dozen jurisdictions, from Comoros and Cameroon to Zanzibar and Palau.

Notably, the Treasury also removed two vessels — HAKUNA MATATA and PINOCCHIO — from the SDN List after they were sold to non-sanctioned operators, a reminder that the list is meant to be reversible if ships leave the network.
sections.whyItMatters: Designating hulls, not barrels, is the mechanism that actually bites: once a tanker is listed, its insurers, financiers and clearing banks step back. It is a slower squeeze than a blockade but a more durable one — and it targets the Chinese-linked companies that keep the trade alive.

sections.heading: Hormuz: Tanker Attacks Hit a Wartime High, but a Cautious Corridor Emerges
sections.body:
Most Gulf stock markets closed lower on Thursday as tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz hit a wartime high, according to Reuters, with deadly strikes on Saudi airports widening the conflict and stalled US-Iran diplomacy offering investors little relief. Iran's Revolutionary Guards also announced a maritime restricted zone stretching from Chabahar into the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea, warning that vessels transiting without coordinating with Iran would face consequences, per Fars news agency via Hellenic Shipping News.

Against that backdrop, a tentative diplomatic track has opened: Iran and Oman have reached a preliminary agreement on a 'joint temporary navigational corridor' through Hormuz, including coordinated mine-clearing and traffic management, according to regional logistics outlet Transport and Logistics ME. Iran has stressed the corridor is interim, not a full reopening, and that broader access remains conditional on sanctions relief and its standoff with Washington. Oman, a traditional neutral mediator, has pushed the phased approach.
sections.whyItMatters: The gap between escalating attacks and a phased corridor tells you Tehran is trying to convert disruption into negotiating chips rather than close the strait outright. The corridor, if it holds, would be the first concrete supply relief in months — but it is fragile and condition-dependent.

sections.heading: Only One Commodity Vessel Left Hormuz on Wednesday
sections.body:
The scale of the disruption is stark: energy outlet OilPrice.com reports that just one commodity vessel left the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday. A UK Joint Maritime Information Center assessment cited by the Jamestown Foundation's China Brief keeps the threat level at SEVERE, the highest on its scale, with commercial traffic in the single digits per direction against a 2025 historical average of roughly 138 vessels per day.

The IMF-relevant backdrop: Hormuz normally handles about a fifth of global oil and gas shipments. Iran's pressure is not stable management of traffic but the ability to raise risk until operators stay away.
sections.whyItMatters: A near-empty strait is the single clearest signal that the conflict is still constraining physical supply, regardless of what futures prices say. It keeps a floor under freight and insurance costs even when crude benchmarks wobble.

sections.heading: Iraq Trades Deep Discounts for Ships as China Swaps Iranian for Iraqi Crude
sections.body:
Iraq is using aggressive pricing to keep barrels moving. OilPrice.com reports that trading house Vitol bought at least 25 million barrels of September-loading Iraqi crude, and ADNOC bought another 40 million barrels, after Baghdad's SOMO offered discounts of $15 to $20.80 per barrel to official selling prices. Because Iraq lacks its own large tanker fleet, the discount effectively buys shipping capacity through a risky strait.

Arab News, citing Reuters and Middle East Economic Survey analyst Yesar Al-Maleki, reports that Chinese independent 'teapot' refineries have closed deals for up to 20 million barrels of Iraqi and Qatari crude for October and November, replacing sanctioned Iranian supply. Al-Maleki notes Iraq has offered discounts of up to $37 a barrel to compensate buyers for the risk of transiting Hormuz. Chinese purchases were already about 1.2 million bpd of Iraqi crude before the war.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the trade's quiet rebalancing. Washington's blockade is pushing China toward Iraqi and Qatari barrels rather than Iranian ones — good for Baghdad's finances, painful for Tehran, and a shift that partially insulates Beijing from the oil shock.

sections.heading: Europe's Winter Risk: TTF Jumps 4% as Storage Sits Two-Thirds Full
sections.body: Europe's benchmark TTF gas price jumped 4% at the open in Amsterdam on Thursday (September 24 print, per OilPrice.com) as the US-Iran standoff kept LNG shipments blocked, before easing to about $84.30 per MWh. Prices had peaked earlier in the month near $93 per MWh, the highest since January 2023. Hormuz accounted for about 20% of global LNG supply before the conflict. Fitch Ratings notes EU gas storage is only two-thirds full — enough to avoid disruption but well below the 80-90% levels seen in 2022-2025.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe enters winter with a thin buffer and a Middle East supply chokepoint still blocked. Any cold snap or further escalation turns a manageable storage position into a price spike; the LNG market has less spare flexibility than the crude market.

sections.heading: China Wields Rare Earths Into January as the Truce Clock Ticks
sections.body: China's rare-earth export controls remain the central non-energy lever in its trade standoff with Washington. A two-month truce between Washington and Beijing — reported by MSN's market coverage — puts US magnet producers MP Materials, USA Rare Earth and Lynas on a 'January 10 clock,' with August shipments still under pressure. The EU Institute for Security Studies warns that talk of a US-China 'trade truce' risks lulling Europe into complacency, arguing Beijing's controls on rare earths and critical materials 'remain disruptive, unpredictable and coercive.'
sections.whyItMatters: Critical-minerals leverage is the mirror image of the oil chokepoint game: China can squeeze Western defense and chip supply chains without firing a shot. The January deadline gives both sides a hard deadline, and Europe is the exposed bystander.

bottomLine: Washington's designation of 17 shadow-fleet tankers is the day's clearest move: it targets the hulls and Chinese-linked owners that keep Iranian barrels moving, a slower but more durable lever than the naval blockade. Meanwhile Hormuz traffic remains near zero — one commodity vessel departed Wednesday — even as Iran and Oman sketch a fragile temporary corridor. Iraq is filling the gap with steep discounts that pull Chinese teapots away from Iranian crude, and Europe faces winter with gas storage only two-thirds full and TTF prices reacting sharply to every LNG headline. The pressure is landing on Iran's revenue and Europe's winter, and the corridor talks are the variable to watch.
sources: US Treasury OFAC press release (sb0653), Reuters (Gulf stocks), OilPrice.com, Arab News/Reuters (Al-Maleki/MEES), Transport and Logistics ME, Hellenic Shipping News/Fars, Jamestown Foundation China Brief (JMIC), Iraq Oil Report, Fitch Ratings, EU Institute for Security Studies, MSN market coverage
